Describes the received commentary and its extension of the chapter 8 algorithm.

verdicts.finding: MacTutor reports Liu’s own reading and his commentary; Chemla 2008 p.4 relates the transmitted commentary. The third-century range correctly qualifies traditional 263; do not call this first circulation.

source_passages.supports: Dates the Li-led submission and identifies the transmitted commentary.
Identifies the Li group’s subcommentary on Liu Hui and the base text.

verdicts.finding: Chemla 2008 p.4 and 2020 The sources identify the Tang group’s 656 subcommentary on the received Liu layer. This is later scholarly use; composition and transmission layers can be difficult to separate.

source_passages.supports: Records the Li-led commentary’s presentation to the throne in 656.
Identifies it as a subcommentary on both the base text and Liu Hui.

verdicts.finding: 656 court submission supports a narrow scoped availability inference, without claiming that the court read or endorsed it. The separately documented 1084 printing remains a publication. Later Jia Xian use of the ancient layers is also reported in Chemla 2020 but is not used to establish the selected 656 court date.

source_passages.supports: Al-Qurashī commented on Abū Kāmil’s algebra and died in 1184; later sources preserve fragments.

verdicts.finding: Djebbar section 3.1 identifies al-Qurashī’s commentary on Abū Kāmil and death in 1184; limited personal scholarly use is supported by later testimony. His commentary remains lost as an independent text.

source_passages.supports: Lists an Ibn Zakariyā of Granada with a 1407 death date; identification with the commentator named without a full identity in the other account is an inference.

verdicts.finding: The revised by-1407 bound explicitly acknowledges 1404 versus 1407 and that identification with the Granada author remains an inference. The original fragments and identifying manuscript have not been independently examined.

source_passages.locator: Object B6063, date and Type III description
source_passages.supports: Signed multiplication tablet is identified as a student training witness, with Nippur uncertain.

verdicts.finding: The institutional catalogue identifies B6063 as an Old Babylonian Type III school tablet signed “long tablet of Gan-Gal”; its type represents an acquired student skill. Nippur remains tentative, and the modern interpretation of signature and training is not an eyewitness report.

source_passages.supports: The square diagram includes a numerical square-root-of-two approximation and corresponding diagonal value.

verdicts.finding: The catalogue dates YBC 7289 to the Old Babylonian period and identifies the square, diagonal, numerical approximation and product. The scoped inference is use of a written representation, not demonstrated independent computation or a formal theorem.

source_passages.locator: Printed p. 144 / PDF p. 144, Textbook maths
source_passages.supports: Describes the surviving papyrus, its mathematical problems, and approximate date.

source_passages.locator: PDF pp. 17 and 57, description and copyist
source_passages.supports: Identifies Aḥmose as copyist and discusses uncertainties about comprehension.

verdicts.finding: Chace introduction describes Aḥmose’s copy and estimates about 1650 BCE; the British Museum guide p.144 describes the problems and dates it about 1550 BCE. The explicit 1700–1500 BCE approximate bounding envelope is a reviewable accommodation of conflicting estimates, not a proven historical limit. Access is scoped to the copyist; no calculation or broader readership is inferred.

source_passages.supports: The inscription records a garden and uses a small zero mark in 270 and 50.

verdicts.finding: MacTutor states that the 876 inscription records a 187 × 270 garden and 50 garlands with small zero marks. This is evidence of scoped written numerical use, not the first zero or Brahmagupta’s arithmetic rules.

source_passages.supports: The manuscript was copied by Stephen for Arethas in Constantinople in 888.

source_passages.locator: Book VII proposition VII.2 and f. 128
source_passages.supports: Identifies the greatest-common-measure proposition in the same manuscript.

verdicts.finding: Clay identifies D’Orville 301 as Stephen’s 888 Constantinople copy for Arethas and locates Elements VII.2, greatest common measure, on f.128. Access by the copyist is a limited inference; receipt or actual calculation by Arethas is unproved.
